title: List-item enumeration markers
description: This latent fires on the numerals/bullet markers ('2.', '3.', etc.) and lead-in fragments ('By', 'Consider', 'Perhaps a more') that begin an enumerated list item or a suggested-step in advice-giving text, especially at the very start of a step before the substantive content of the step is stated. It activates most strongly on bare enumeration tokens themselves, and more weakly on the opening words of advice sentences ('You could try to...', 'Try to have...', 'By communicating...') that function as the first clause of a suggested action within a numbered or bulleted list of recommendations. It does not activate strongly on full, self-contained advice or reasoning sentences that lack a leading enumerator or list-initial framing (e.g., sentences explaining consequences, validating feelings, or asking questions), even if they discuss the same topic of communication or conflict resolution, since the latent tracks the structural list/step-initiation cue rather than the advice content itself.

title: Pronoun 'It' token
description: This latent fires on the token 'It' (with or without a following contraction like "'s"), typically appearing at or near the start of a sentence. It activates on instances of this specific pronoun used as a subject, regardless of the topic or clause that follows. It would not activate on other pronouns (he, she, they), on 'it' used mid-sentence as an object, or on unrelated words, since the trigger appears tied to this particular lexical token in sentence-initial position.

title: Suggesting social/leisure activities to meet or bond with people
description: This latent fires on advice-style sentences that propose specific social or recreational activities (book clubs, hiking groups, coffee dates, game nights, sports teams, etc.) as ways to meet new people, connect with someone, or spend time together, often phrased as lists of options or suggestions ('This could be a book club, sports team...'; 'Suggest going for a hike or a walk'). It also activates on related questions probing when/where such social encounters happen (e.g., 'Is it during lunch, between classes...?'). It does not activate on general relationship/emotional advice, boundary-setting, conflict resolution, or interpersonal problem-solving text that lacks concrete activity/venue suggestions, even if the topic is also social (e.g., sentences about apologizing, communicating feelings, or setting boundaries do not trigger it).

title: Affirming individual uniqueness
description: This latent fires on generic, affirming statements about individuals possessing unique qualities, talents, or worth, typically framed as universal truisms (e.g., 'everyone has X'). It activates on broad, feel-good generalizations about personal identity or capability rather than specific claims about a particular person. It would not activate on sentences describing a specific individual's concrete skill or achievement, technical descriptions of abilities, or statements lacking the inclusive/universal 'everyone' or 'each person' framing.

title: Affirming self-worth and emotional entitlement
description: This latent fires on statements that validate the listener's right to positive emotional outcomes—happiness, fulfillment, respect—especially in the context of personal relationships. It activates on reassuring, empathetic assertions that counterbalance a preceding concern or hardship by reminding the person of their deservingness or self-worth. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, advice-giving that lacks an affirming/validating tone, or expressions of happiness/fulfillment that are not framed as something the listener 'deserves' or is entitled to. It is distinct from general emotional support language that doesn't invoke worthiness or deservingness explicitly.

title: Affirming self-worth reassurance
description: This latent fires on supportive, therapist-like statements that affirm the listener's inherent worth, emotional well-being, and right to prioritize themselves, typically in the context of relationship or interpersonal struggles. It activates on second-person reassurances that open with framing like 'Remember,' 'It's important/great/essential,' and center on validating the person's value, boundaries, or feelings independent of others' actions. It would not activate on neutral advice-giving, factual statements about relationships, or third-person descriptions of self-esteem that lack this direct, comforting, affirmation-of-worth address to 'you.'

title: Reframing vulnerability as strength
description: This latent activates on encouraging statements that reframe self-care, emotional needs, or perceived weaknesses as actually being signs of strength, courage, or resilience. It fires on affirming, supportive language that counters a negative self-perception (e.g., 'X is not a weakness, it's a strength') often paired with an imperative or reminder tone ('Remember...'). It would not activate on neutral advice-giving, factual statements about emotions, or generic motivational quotes that lack this specific reframing move from weakness to strength.

title: Therapeutic reassurance about emotional healing
description: This latent fires on supportive, empathetic language that reassures someone they can process difficult emotions and heal over time, often using phrases like 'move forward', 'heal', 'take time', and 'process your emotions'. It activates on sentences with a soothing, encouraging tone typical of counseling or self-help advice, emphasizing patience and eventual emotional recovery. It would not activate on neutral descriptions of emotions, clinical/diagnostic discussions of mental health, or advice-giving that lacks this gentle, validating, forward-looking framing (e.g., blunt instructions or factual statements about grief without reassurance).

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens that begin items in an enumerated or ordered list (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.'), often followed by bolded headers or short phrases. It activates most strongly on the bare digit/period token itself, especially in advice-style or step-by-step responses that break content into numbered points. It does not activate on the prose content of the list items themselves, nor on unnumbered bullet points, headers without numerals, or general narrative sentences that lack an explicit ordinal marker.

title: Formulaic exclamatory opener naming a dilemma/topic
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory or introductory phrases—often a single noun phrase followed by an exclamation point or period—that label the upcoming content as a dilemma, conundrum, drama, question, debate, thread, post, or greeting (e.g. 'The age-old dilemma!', 'What a conundrum!', 'Hello there!'). These act as stock rhetorical openers or reactions signaling the tone of the response before substantive content is given, frequently in advice-column or Reddit-style replies. It does not activate on the substantive advice, reasoning, or content itself (e.g. sentences giving actual recommendations, explanations, validations, or step-by-step suggestions), even when those sentences discuss the same dilemma-related topics—only the brief framing/labeling exclamation triggers strong activation, with weaker activation on similar but more embedded or descriptive uses of 'dilemma'-type phrasing within longer sentences.

title: Blunt verdict statements
description: This latent fires on short, declarative verdict sentences that pronounce a clear moral judgment on someone's behavior in an interpersonal conflict, typically in the pattern '[Person]'s [behavior/reaction/response] was [negative adjective]' (e.g., 'unacceptable', 'unreasonable and entitled', 'ridiculous', 'aggressive and entitled'). It also activates strongly on bare numeral list markers ('2.', '3.') that introduce enumerated points in advice responses, suggesting the latent tracks the structural moment of delivering a concise, standalone conclusion or ruling rather than elaboration. It does not activate on longer hedged, explanatory, or empathetic sentences that qualify, contextualize, or soften a judgment (e.g., 'it's understandable that...', 'however, it's also important to consider...'), even when discussing the same interpersonal-conflict topics—those instead invoke reasoning/empathy-oriented latents rather than this terse-verdict one.
